title_en: Zhuhai A Industrial Development Co., Ltd. v. Bo B Enterprise Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over tort liability
ruling_gist_en: Article 535, paragraph 1 of the Civil Code provides that the object of an obligee's subrogation right is the counterparty of the debtor. The counterparty of the debtor as prescribed in this article refers to a civil subject that has a direct legal relationship with the debtor, and shall be limited to the debtor's debtor, and shall not be extensively interpreted to include the debtor's sub-debtor or even subsequent debtors. An obligee cannot assert claims against the debtor's sub-debtor or even subsequent debtors through two levels of subrogation.
keywords_en: civil; tort liability dispute; obligee's subrogation right dispute; first instance; Supreme People's Court; Guangdong Province; Shanghai Municipality; legal person; foreign-invested enterprise; Civil Code; Enterprise Bankruptcy Law; whether the object of subrogation includes sub-debtors; effect of reorganization plan on joint and several debtors; preconditions for individual creditor representative litigation; obligee's subrogation right; bankruptcy reorganization; equity transfer; joint and several debt; tort liability; bankruptcy; dispute over tort liability with a certain industry limited company, et al.
full_text_en:
Dispute between Zhuhai a Certain Industrial Development Co., Ltd. and P* Enterprise Co., Ltd. et al. over Tort Liability

Ruling Summary

1. Paragraph 1 of Article 535 of the Civil Code provides that the object of the creditor's subrogation right is the counterparty of the debtor. The debtor's counterparty stipulated in this Article refers to a civil subject that has a direct legal relationship with the debtor, and shall be limited to the debtor's debtor; it cannot be interpreted expansively to include the debtor's sub-debtor or even further downstream debtors. A creditor cannot claim debts from the debtor's sub-debtor or even further downstream debtors through double-layer subrogation.

2. A reorganization plan approved by a court order binds only the debtor and all creditors. The rights of a creditor against other joint and several debtors are not affected by the reorganization plan, and the plan cannot prevent the creditor from continuing to claim satisfaction from other joint and several debtors for the portion of the debt not satisfied by the bankrupt enterprise.

3. Where a creditor requests the administrator to recover the debtor's property from sub-debtors, capital contributors of the debtor, etc., in accordance with the law, but the administrator fails to do so, and an individual creditor, pursuant to paragraph 3 of Article 23 of the Judicial Interpretation II of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law, institutes an action on behalf of all creditors against the sub-debtors or capital contributors of the debtor, demanding that they pay or return property to the debtor, the people's court shall accept the case. Whether an individual creditor has obtained the consent or authorization of all creditors through the creditors' meeting or the creditors' committee to institute the action is not a prerequisite for filing the lawsuit.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2024) Supreme People's Court Commercial First Instance No. 2

Plaintiff: Zhuhai a Certain Industrial Development Co., Ltd. Domicile: Hengqin New District, Zhuhai City, Guangdong Province, the People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Bai Mou, Executive Director of the company.

Agent ad litem: Xu Xiaoguang, attorney at V&T Alliance (Shenzhen) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Mao Jianwu, attorney at V&T Alliance (Shenzhen) Law Firm.

Defendant: P* Enterprise Co., Ltd. (P* Ent Ltd.). Domicile: Tortola, British Virgin Islands.

Representative: Huang Mou (Huang*), Director of the company.

Agent ad litem: Li Mingle, attorney at Beijing Hanting (Shanghai) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Zhai Xiaoqiang, attorney at Beijing Hanting (Shanghai) Law Firm.

Defendant: P* Fortune, LLC. Domicile: Camden, Delaware, the United States of America.

Representative: Huang Mou (Huang*), Director of the company.

Agent ad litem: Li Mingle, attorney at Beijing Hanting (Shanghai) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wang Bingqian, trainee attorney at Beijing Hanting (Shanghai) Law Firm.

Defendant: P* LP. Domicile: Camden, Delaware, the United States of America.

Representative: Huang Mou (Huang*), Director of the company.

Agent ad litem: Li Mingle, attorney at Beijing Hanting (Shanghai) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Shen Xiaoyue, attorney at Beijing Hanting (Shanghai) Law Firm.

Third Party: Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Co., Ltd. Domicile: Hongkou District, Shanghai, the People's Republic of China.

Bankruptcy Administrator: Shanghai Bangxinyang Zhongjian Zhonghui Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Yuan Xiaobo, attorney at Shanghai Bangxinyang Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Shi Yutian, attorney at Shanghai Bangxinyang Law Firm.

Third Party: Shanghai a Certain Trade Co., Ltd. Domicile: Jinshan District, Shanghai, the People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Lao Mou, Executive Director of the company.

Agent ad litem: Shao Jun, attorney at Shanghai Zhengzheng Law Firm.

In the case of dispute over tort liability between the Plaintiff, Zhuhai a Certain Industrial Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhuhai a Certain Company), and the Defendants, P* Enterprise Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as P* Company), P* Fortune, LLC (hereinafter referred to as P* Fortune), and P* LP (hereinafter referred to as P* LP), the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province (hereinafter referred to as Zhuhai Intermediate Court) accepted the case on December 5, 2022, under case number (2022) Yue 04 Min Chu No. 378. Pursuant to Article 21, paragraph 2, and Article 39, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (as amended in 2021), and Article 2, item 5 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Establishment of International Commercial Courts (2018), this Court issued a civil ruling on December 8, 2023, under case number (2023) Supreme People's Court Min Xia No. 121, ruling that this case shall be tried by the First International Commercial Court of this Court. After this Court accepted the case on March 11, 2024, it formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law to try the case. Before the trial of this case, Zhuhai a Certain Company changed its claims to a creditor's subrogation action and applied to add Shanghai a Certain Trade Co., Ltd. (formerly known as Shanghai a Certain Network Technology Co., Ltd., hereinafter referred to as Shanghai a Certain Trade Company) as a third party, which this Court granted. Because this case is a creditor's subrogation action, this Court added the debtor, Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company), as a third party. This Court held a public hearing of this case on August 29, 2024. The following persons appeared in court: agents ad litem of the Plaintiff Zhuhai a Certain Company, Xu Xiaoguang and Mao Jianwu; agent ad litem of the Defendants P* Company and P* LP, Li Mingle; agents ad litem of the Defendant P* Fortune, Li Mingle and Wang Bingqian; the responsible person of the bankruptcy administrator of the third party Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, Wang Mou, and its agents ad litem Yuan Xiaobo and Shi Yutian; and the agent ad litem of the third party Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, Shao Jun. This case is now concluded.

Zhuhai a Certain Company filed a lawsuit with the Zhuhai Intermediate Court, requesting: 1. An order that the three defendants, P* Company, P* Fortune, and P* LP (hereinafter referred to as the three defendants), jointly compensate Zhuhai a Certain Company in the amount of RMB 80,393,631.08 (unless otherwise specified, all amounts are in RMB, calculated up to November 28, 2022); 2. An order that the three defendants jointly compensate Zhuhai a Certain Company for the interest losses on the principal amount of RMB 37,000,000 at a monthly interest rate of 2% from November 28, 2022, until the date of actual payment; 3. All litigation costs of this case shall be borne by the three defendants. Facts and Reasons: Zhuhai a Certain Company holds a creditor's right against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company. Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company wholly owns Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, which in turn wholly owns J* Limited (hereinafter referred to as J* Company). The three defendants colluded and conspired with Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company to transfer, by way of equity transfer, all of the equity held by Shanghai a Certain Trade Company in J* Company to the three defendants free of charge, thereby stripping the assets of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, which remains unable to pay its debt of RMB 1.445 billion owed to Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, consequently rendering Zhuhai a Certain Company's creditor's right unenforceable. The conduct of the three defendants intentionally harmed the interests of Zhuhai a Certain Company, constituting a tort against Zhuhai a Certain Company's creditor's right against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, and they should compensate for the corresponding losses caused by the inability to realize Zhuhai a Certain Company's creditor's right.

After this Court accepted the case, Zhuhai a Certain Company applied on May 20, 2024, to add Shanghai a Certain Trade Company as a defendant, to bear joint liability with the aforementioned three defendants, and changed the grounds of the action to first confirm the invalidity of the set-off of the creditor's right of RMB 1.445 billion that Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company held against Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, and then, based on this, claim that Shanghai a Certain Trade Company's transfer of equity in J* Company to the three defendants free of charge constituted a tort against Zhuhai a Certain Company's creditor's right.

After this Court organized the parties to exchange evidence on May 28, 2024, Zhuhai a Certain Company submitted another application on June 11, changing the addition of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company as a third party and amending its claims to: 1. An order that the three defendants jointly pay Zhuhai a Certain Company RMB 61,227,031.74. The aforementioned creditor's right shall be included in the bankruptcy estate of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, to be distributed fairly among all creditors in accordance with the law; 2. After the performance of the above payment obligation, the corresponding amounts of the creditor-debtor relationships between Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company and Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, and between Shanghai a Certain Trade Company and the three defendants, shall be extinguished; 3. The litigation costs of this case shall be borne by the three defendants. The main facts and reasons are as follows:

(i) Zhuhai a Certain Company holds a lawful creditor's right against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company. The interest on the creditor's right has ceased to accrue, and the unpaid amount is RMB 61,227,031.74. 1. The creditor's right of Zhuhai a Certain Company against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company has been confirmed by an effective arbitral award. On January 5, 2018, Zhuhai a Certain Company lent RMB 37,000,000 to Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, with an unrelated party, Zhejiang a Certain Fiber Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhejiang a Certain Fiber Company), among others, providing joint and several guarantee. On February 18, 2019, the Beijing Arbitration Commission issued Award (2019) Jing Zhong Cai Zi No. 0342, ordering Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company to repay the principal of RMB 37,000,000 plus interest, attorney's fees, and arbitration costs. The four guarantors, including Zhejiang a Certain Fiber Company, are jointly and severally liable for the above debts. Zhuhai a Certain Company applied for compulsory enforcement of the award to the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Shanghai Second Intermediate Court) but did not recover any property. 2. Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company has entered bankruptcy proceedings, and the interest on Zhuhai a Certain Company's creditor's right has ceased to accrue. On October 19, 2022, the Shanghai Third Intermediate People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Shanghai Third Intermediate Court) accepted the bankruptcy liquidation case of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company. Zhuhai a Certain Company declared a creditor's right of RMB 80,281,110.53 to the administrator of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, which was confirmed as an unsecured ordinary claim. 3. Zhuhai a Certain Company's creditor's right has been partially satisfied. On October 28, 2022, the Huzhou Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province (hereinafter referred to as Huzhou Intermediate Court) accepted the bankruptcy reorganization application of Zhejiang a Certain Fiber Company. On March 10, 2023, the Huzhou Intermediate Court confirmed that Zhuhai a Certain Company holds an ordinary claim of RMB 80,478,443.86 against Zhejiang a Certain Fiber Company. On October 17, 2023, Zhuhai a Certain Company received a cash payment of RMB 8,047,844.39 from Zhejiang a Certain Fiber Company by bank transfer, and on October 27, received 2,092,440 shares of Zhejiang a Certain Fiber Company stock, with a closing price of RMB 5.26 per share on that day. Thus, Zhuhai a Certain Company has received a total actual satisfaction of RMB 19,054,078.79, and the remaining creditor's right amount is RMB 61,227,031.74.

(ii) Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company holds a matured creditor's right of over RMB 1.1 billion against Shanghai a Certain Trade Company. As of April 23, 2020, Shanghai a Certain Trade Company owed Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company a matured debt of RMB 1.445 billion. Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company announced that on March 25, 2021, Shanghai a Certain Trade Company acquired from former China Minsheng Trust Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Minsheng Trust) and Huarong International Trust Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huarong Trust) two claims against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company. As of September 24, 2021, the total amount of these two claims was RMB 1,546,870,282.09. After repaying Shanghai a Certain Trade Company's debt of RMB 1.445 billion to Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, there remained a surplus of RMB 219,062,536.34. Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company acknowledges that the debts that were not genuine, used to "repay" genuine claims, are invalid, and the balance of its creditor's right against Shanghai a Certain Trade Company remains over RMB 1.1 billion. The civil ruling of the Shanghai Third Intermediate Court confirming the creditor's right in the bankruptcy proceedings does not have substantive res judicata effect. First, the amount of the two claims used by Shanghai a Certain Trade Company to "repay" its debts was seriously inflated and falsely recorded. According to the enforcement ruling and the enforcement certificate issued on April 17, 2020, based on the statutory upper limit of the annualized interest rate of 24%, as of September 24, 2021, the balance of Huarong Trust and Minsheng Trust claims totaled RMB 932,969,574.39, but Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company and Shanghai a Certain Trade Company falsely recorded the balance as RMB 1.547 billion. Second, with respect to the RMB 610 million Huarong Trust claim acquired by Shanghai a Certain Trade Company free of charge, according to Article 14 of the Judicial Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Security System under the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China, where Shanghai a Certain Trade Company has not assumed the guarantee liability, it has no right to assert this RMB 610 million claim (falsely recorded as approximately RMB 800 million) against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, nor can it use it to repay its debts.

(iii) Shanghai a Certain Trade Company holds a matured creditor's right of USD 530 million against the three defendants. J* Company is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company. During the period 2019-2020, the three defendants and Shanghai a Certain Trade Company successively entered into a "Share Transfer Agreement" and several supplementary agreements, stipulating that the three defendants would purchase 100% of the equity in J* Company held by Shanghai a Certain Trade Company for USD 530 million. Shanghai a Certain Trade Company agreed to deliver the equity in J* Company to the three defendants first on April 17, 2020, while the payment obligation of the three defendants was deferred until September 24, 2021. In another lawsuit filed by P* LP in the UK courts, it claimed that it had already acquired all the equity in J* Company and would resell it externally. The three defendants have received the equity in J* Company but have not paid the USD 530 million equity transfer price to Shanghai a Certain Trade Company.

(iv) As a creditor of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company has the right to subrogate the claim of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company against the three defendants and demand that the three defendants satisfy the claim directly to Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company. Pursuant to Articles 535 and 537 of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Civil Code), the debtor, Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, has neglected to exercise its matured claim of USD 530 million against the three defendants, thereby affecting the realization of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company's matured claim of over RMB 1.1 billion. The creditor, Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, has the right to subrogate the rights of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company against the three defendants in its own name.

(v) The administrator has not pursued claims against Shanghai a Certain Trade Company and the three defendants, so Zhuhai a Certain Company has the right to sue the three defendants on behalf of all creditors of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company. After the exchange of evidence in this case, several creditors of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company requested the administrator to subrogate the rights against the three defendants and recover bankruptcy property, but the administrator did not respond. Pursuant to Articles 21 and 23 of the Judicial Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the People's Republic of China (II) (hereinafter referred to as Judicial Interpretation II of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law), if the administrator refuses to recover the claims of the bankrupt enterprise, an individual creditor may sue on behalf of all creditors, demanding that the sub-debtor or other relevant obligors satisfy the claim to the bankrupt enterprise. Although bankruptcy derivative actions are subject to centralized jurisdiction by the bankruptcy court, a higher court still has the power to transfer the case up for trial. This case is a foreign-related commercial dispute derived from the bankruptcy proceedings of a former A-share listed company, has typical significance, and has been transferred up for trial by the Supreme People's Court, which has jurisdiction.

The three defendants responded in their defense: Zhuhai a Certain Company's claims are contradictory and, in fact, aimed at concealing the fact that it has no direct interest in this case, and the claims should be dismissed. (i) Zhuhai a Certain Company has no right to initiate this lawsuit against the three defendants. 1. Zhuhai a Certain Company has no right to bypass the administrator and bring this action on behalf of all creditors of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company. Zhuhai a Certain Company filed this action on November 28, 2022. Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company had already entered bankruptcy proceedings on October 19, 2022. Zhuhai a Certain Company did not, through the creditors' meeting or the creditors' committee, request the administrator to recover claims from Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, nor did it obtain authorization from all creditors of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company to file the subrogation action. The amount claimed by Zhuhai a Certain Company is the amount of its own claim against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, not the amount of the claim that Zhuhai a Certain Company alleges Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company holds against Shanghai a Certain Trade Company. Pursuant to Article 23 of Judicial Interpretation II of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law, Zhuhai a Certain Company is not entitled to bring this action on behalf of all creditors of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company. Moreover, Zhuhai a Certain Company has been fully satisfied through the debt-to-equity swap in the bankruptcy reorganization proceedings of the guarantor, Zhejiang a Certain Fiber Company. 2. Zhuhai a Certain Company has no right to bring this action against the three defendants through double-layer subrogation. The Civil Code does not provide that a creditor may subrogate through multiple layers of debtors. Zhuhai a Certain Company's action, which leaps over two tiers of debtors, Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company and Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, to sue the three defendants directly, constitutes double-layer subrogation, which does not comply with Article 535 of the Civil Code. (ii) The three defendants are not obliged to pay any so-called equity transfer price to Shanghai a Certain Trade Company. On June 12, 2020, Shanghai a Certain Trade Company applied to the High Court of England and Wales for an injunction prohibiting the transfer of the subject equity to P* LP. In that litigation, P* LP, Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, and other parties reached a settlement, and P* LP terminated the acquisition of the subject equity. Therefore, the three defendants are not required to pay any so-called equity transfer price to Shanghai a Certain Trade Company. The shareholders of J* Company have never changed to the three defendants, and there is no fact as alleged by Zhuhai a Certain Company that the three defendants received the subject equity and then directly resold it. (iii) Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company is not a creditor of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company but rather a debtor of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company. The set-off of claims and debts between Shanghai a Certain Trade Company and Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, and the resulting claim of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company, have been recognized by the administrator and confirmed by the civil ruling of the court that accepted the bankruptcy application. Zhuhai a Certain Company's assertion that the set-off is invalid lacks basis. The fact that Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, as a guarantor of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company's debt, acquired a claim against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company from Beijing a Certain Building Materials Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Beijing a Certain Building Materials Company) and then used it to offset its other debts to Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company does not violate Article 14 of the Judicial Interpretation on the Application of the Security System under the Civil Code, and its validity should be recognized. (iv) The set-off between Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company and Shanghai a Certain Trade Company, and the amount of the claim of Shanghai a Certain Trade Company against Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company after the set-off, are matters of claim confirmation in the bankruptcy case of Shanghai a Certain Entertainment Company and are not within the scope of review in this case. If Zhuhai a Certain Company disputes this amount, it should file a bankruptcy claim confirmation (dispute) action. In summary, the defendants request the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims in accordance with the law.

Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company submitted: (1) The Shanghai Third Intermediate People's Court confirmed that the amount of bankruptcy claim that Zhuhai Mou Company holds against Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company is RMB 79,713,777.20. According to the evidence submitted in this case, Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company has already satisfied the debt of the unauthorized guarantee owed to Zhuhai Mou Company in accordance with the ordinary claim settlement plan under the reorganization plan. Under the reorganization plan, the repayment rate for ordinary claims of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company is 100%. That is, the claim held by Zhuhai Mou Company, with Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company as the primary obligor and Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company as one of the guarantors, has been fully satisfied through the reorganization plan of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company. The administrator of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company was previously unaware of this situation, and Zhuhai Mou Company has never disclosed such satisfaction to the administrator. (2) Based on the documents taken over and the report of claim by Shanghai Mou Trading Company, the administrator of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company confirmed that the amount of bankruptcy claim that Shanghai Mou Trading Company holds against Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company is RMB 238,388,053.20. Upon verification, this claim was obtained after the setoff of receivables and payables between the parties, and the setoff was approved by the board of directors meeting and shareholders' general meeting of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company and was publicly announced by Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company. (3) Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company is not aware of the creditor-debtor relationship between Shanghai Mou Trading Company and the three defendants, and the administrator has not taken over any documents related to this transaction. If, after trial, the court finds that the enforcement ruling made by the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court has fully set off the principal arrears owed by Huarong Trust and Minsheng Trust under the Trust Loan Contract, and that the total amount of interest, liquidated damages, penalty interest, compound interest, etc., shall not exceed the annual interest rate of 24%, the administrator may readjust the amount of the claim already recognized by Shanghai Mou Trading Company based on the court's trial and findings in this case. (4) Zhuhai Mou Company has never requested the administrator to recover debtor property through a creditors' meeting or creditors' committee. It was not until June 6, 2024, that it sent a letter to the administrator stating that Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company's debtor had cash deposit assets of USD 6.67 million and that the administrator should immediately file a lawsuit and apply for preservation. The administrator informed Zhuhai Mou Company on July 4, 2024, that it would not recover. According to Article 23 of the Judicial Interpretation II on the Bankruptcy Law, the property recovered by Zhuhai Mou Company in this case shall be included in the debtor's property.

Shanghai Mou Trading Company submitted: (1) On October 19, 2022, the Shanghai Third Intermediate People's Court ruled to accept the bankruptcy liquidation case of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company. On November 28, 2022, Zhuhai Mou Company filed this lawsuit, and the court should not accept it. (2) The cause of action in this case should be a cause related to bankruptcy, not a dispute over creditor's subrogation under contract disputes. If Zhuhai Mou Company disagrees with the claims recorded in the claims table, it should file a lawsuit for confirmation of bankruptcy claims with the court accepting the bankruptcy application, not a creditor's subrogation action. Zhuhai Mou Company's claims both seek payment of RMB 61,227,031.74 from the three defendants to itself and that such amount be included in the bankruptcy estate of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company for fair distribution among all creditors. These claims are contradictory and unclear. (3) According to the Judicial Interpretation II on the Bankruptcy Law, if Zhuhai Mou Company brings this lawsuit on behalf of all creditors, it must fulfill a prerequisite procedure, i.e., request the administrator through the creditors' meeting or creditors' committee to recover debtor property in accordance with the law and obtain corresponding authorization to represent all creditors. Zhuhai Mou Company has no evidence that it fulfilled such prerequisite procedure. (4) Zhuhai Mou Company's two subrogation actions against the three defendants in this case have no clear legal basis. Moreover, after a bankruptcy application is accepted, the people's court should not accept any property lawsuit filed. (5) The enforcement certificates notarized by Huarong Trust and Minsheng Trust both state that principal and interest continue to accrue until the date when all amounts payable are fully paid, not until the date when the principal is fully paid off. Zhuhai Mou Company's position that the claim transferred to Shanghai Mou Trading Company cannot be used to satisfy its liabilities to Shanghai Mou Trading Company constitutes an error in the application of law. Zhuhai Mou Company's claims should be rejected.

The following facts are found by this court upon trial:

(1) Origin and satisfaction of Zhuhai Mou Company's claim

On February 18, 2019, the Beijing Arbitration Commission issued Award (2019) Jing Zhong Zi No. 0342, ruling that Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company should repay loan principal of RMB 37 million and corresponding interest, attorney fees, arbitration fees, and other expenses to Zhuhai Mou Company. Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company and others shall bear joint and several liability for the above debts of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company. Because Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company failed to perform the award, Zhuhai Mou Company applied for compulsory enforcement to the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court. Due to lack of property available for enforcement, on July 13, 2020, the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court issued Enforcement Ruling (2020) Hu 02 Zhi No. 672-1, terminating the enforcement proceedings against some of the guarantors for the above claim. On July 12, 2022, the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court sent a Notice of Case Closure of Enforcement (2019) Hu 02 Zhi No. 404 to Zhuhai Mou Company, informing it that no property had been enforced up to that date.

On October 28, 2022, the Huzhou Intermediate People's Court issued Civil Ruling (2022) Zhe 05 Po Shen No. 1, accepting the bankruptcy reorganization application filed by another creditor against Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company. On November 29, 2022, the Huzhou Intermediate People's Court ruled to approve the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company). On December 27, 2022, the Huzhou Intermediate People's Court ruled to confirm that the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company had been fully executed and terminated the reorganization proceedings of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company. On March 10, 2023, the Huzhou Intermediate People's Court ruled to confirm that Zhuhai Mou Company held an ordinary claim of RMB 80,478,443.86. According to the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company, ordinary claims of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company would be satisfied through a combination of cash consideration paid by the reorganizing investor, retained debt, shares used for debt repayment under the equity holder rights adjustment plan, and trust beneficiary interest units. For claims satisfied by shares issued from capital reserve capitalization, the share price for debt satisfaction was RMB 27.8 per share. The repayment rate for ordinary claims of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company was 100%. According to the Guangfa Online Banking Electronic Receipt generated on October 17, 2023, Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company paid RMB 8,047,844.39 to Zhuhai Mou Company, with the remark "Debt satisfaction payment under reorganization of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Co., Ltd." According to the screenshot of the stock delivery receipt provided by Zhuhai Mou Company, on October 27, 2023, Zhuhai Mou Company received 2,092,440 shares of Zhejiang Mou Fiber Company at a transaction price of RMB 5.26 per share.

(2) Creditor-debtor relationship between Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company and Shanghai Mou Trading Company

On November 13, 2017, Minsheng Trust and Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company entered into a Trust Loan Contract. On February 5, 2018, the Beijing Fangyuan Notary Public Office, upon application by Minsheng Trust, issued Enforcement Certificate (2018) Jing Fangyuan Zhi Zi No. 0028, with the person subject to enforcement being Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company and others. The enforcement certificate confirmed the subject matter of enforcement as: remaining payable amount of RMB 792,255,555.56 as well as liquidated damages, penalty interest, and notary fees, with the said liquidated damages and penalty interest limited to what is protected by law.

On August 18, 2017, Huarong Trust and Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company entered into a Trust Loan Contract. On February 27, 2018, the Beijing Fangyuan Notary Public Office, upon application by Huarong Trust, issued Notarial Certificate (2018) Jing Fangyuan Zhi Zi No. 0037, with the persons subject to enforcement being Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company, Shanghai Mou Trading Company, and others. The notarial certificate confirmed the subject matter of enforcement as: remaining payable principal amount of RMB 1.11 billion as well as interest, compound interest, penalty interest, liquidated damages, and notary fees, with the total of the said interest, compound interest, penalty interest, and liquidated damages limited to the amount protected by law.

On April 17, 2020, the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court issued Enforcement Rulings (2018) Hu 02 Zhi No. 149-2 and (2018) Hu 02 Zhi No. 115-2 respectively, ordering that the 55% equity interest in Shanghai Mou Trading Company held by Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company be delivered to the applying enforcement creditor Huarong Trust in satisfaction of principal arrears and related interest and notary fees, and that the 45% equity interest in Shanghai Mou Trading Company held by Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company be delivered to the applying enforcement creditor Minsheng Trust in satisfaction of principal arrears and related interest.

On December 6, 2021, Shanghai Mou Trading Company and Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company signed a Receivables and Payables Setoff Agreement. The agreement provided that: On December 4, 2020, Huarong Trust transferred its rights and interests under the Trust Loan Contract against Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company to Minsheng Trust. On February 20, 2021, Minsheng Trust transferred its rights and interests under the two Trust Loan Contracts against Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company to Beijing Mou Building Materials Company. On March 25, 2021, Beijing Mou Building Materials Company transferred its rights and interests under the two Trust Loan Contracts against Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company to Shanghai Mou Trading Company. As of September 24, 2021, Shanghai Mou Trading Company owed Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company RMB 1,327,807,745.75, and Shanghai Mou Trading Company was owed by Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company RMB 1,546,870,282.09. Both parties agreed to set off the above receivables and payables, and after such setoff, Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company still needed to pay Shanghai Mou Trading Company RMB 219,062,536.34 and corresponding interest.

(3) Bankruptcy-related circumstances of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company

Because Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company was unable to pay its due debts, another creditor applied to the Shanghai Third Intermediate People's Court for bankruptcy liquidation of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company. On October 19, 2022, that court issued Ruling (2022) Hu 03 Po No. 420, ruling to accept the bankruptcy liquidation application against Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company, and on October 25, 2022, issued Decision (2022) Hu 03 Po No. 420 appointing a bankruptcy administrator.

On December 16, 2022, the administrator of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company issued the Report on Verification of Claims by Creditors' Meeting in the Bankruptcy Liquidation Case of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company. The Report's attached Claims Table of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company showed that the claim filed by Zhuhai Mou Company with serial number FK020 was ordinary in nature, with the filed amount being RMB 80,281,110.53 and the confirmed amount being RMB 79,713,777.20. The claim filed by Shanghai Mou Trading Company with serial number FK002 was ordinary in nature, with the filed amount being RMB 238,388,053.20 and the confirmed amount indicated as "postponed for confirmation," with a remark "pending supplementary submission of documents of transferred claim by the creditor under review."

On March 16, 2023, the Shanghai Third Intermediate People's Court issued Civil Ruling (2022) Hu 03 Po No. 420, confirming the amount of Zhuhai Mou Company's claim as RMB 79,713,777.20. On May 13, 2024, the Shanghai Third Intermediate People's Court issued Civil Ruling (2022) Hu 03 Po No. 420, confirming the amount of Shanghai Mou Trading Company's claim as RMB 238,388,053.20.

(4) Creditor-debtor relationship between Shanghai Mou Trading Company and the three defendants

On June 27, 2019, the three defendants and Shanghai Mou Trading Company signed a Share Transfer Agreement, stipulating that Shanghai Mou Trading Company would transfer 100% of the equity interests of J* Company to BoMou Partnership, and the date when Shanghai Mou Trading Company delivered the original share certificates of the target company to the counterparty would be the delivery date of asset transfer, with the transaction price being USD 530 million. Thereafter, the parties successively signed several supplementary agreements. According to the Announcement of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company Regarding Receipt of a Letter of Notification from the Former Executive Director and Legal Representative of Shanghai Mou Trading Company, the fourth supplementary agreement added a reverse transfer clause: if BoMou Partnership failed to pay the full price on time, the transaction would terminate, and BoMou Partnership would return all reverse transfer delivery documents to Shanghai Mou Trading Company.

Shanghai Mou Trading Company filed a lawsuit in the High Court of England and Wales, seeking a declaration that it still retained ownership of all shares in J* Company, and requesting that the court issue a final injunction prohibiting any amendment to the shareholder register of J* Company and any transaction in the shares of that company. On June 12, 2020, that court issued an injunction. On December 18, 2020, the High Court of England and Wales issued an order staying further proceedings in this action and revoking the previously issued injunction and the order for additional security.

According to the 2020 annual return and the 2021 annual return of J* Company filed with the UK Companies House, the shareholders of J* Company did not change in 2020, and on January 8, 2021, 1,126,753,630 ordinary shares of J* Company were transferred to J*UK.

On September 26, 2021, Shanghai Mou Network Technology Co., Ltd. changed its name to Shanghai Mou Trading Co., Ltd.

Separately, it is found that on July 1, 2024, the administrator of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company submitted a Response Opinion to this court, stating that on June 6, 2024, Zhuhai Mou Company sent an email to the administrator titled "Letter Concerning That the Debtor of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company Has Cash Deposit Assets of USD 6.67 Million and the Administrator Should Immediately File a Lawsuit and Apply for Preservation." After receiving the letter, the administrator conducted a review and concluded that the situation reported by Zhuhai Mou Company was inconsistent with the information previously known to the administrator and the claim review already conducted. Regarding the claim filed by Shanghai Mou Trading Company, Zhuhai Mou Company had not raised any objection during the verification by the creditors' meeting and had never submitted any claim objection to the administrator. The claim of Shanghai Mou Trading Company had already been confirmed by a ruling of the Shanghai Third Intermediate People's Court. Additionally, filing a lawsuit would involve litigation costs and expenses and would also have a certain impact on the ongoing bankruptcy reorganization proceedings. The administrator clearly indicated that it would not pursue recovery.

During the trial, all parties had no objection to the above facts. The above facts are supported by evidence including the arbitration award, effective court judgments and rulings, announcements of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company, documents published on the official website of the UK Companies House, documents issued by audit institutions, independent financial advisors, and special legal advisors, as well as the statements of the parties.

During the trial, the parties unanimously agreed that the laws of the People's Republic of China shall apply to this case. However, matters concerning the registration of shares of J* Company shall be governed by the laws of the place of incorporation of the company.

During the trial of this case, Zhuhai Mou Company applied to this court to investigate and collect evidence regarding the bank account transaction details and the historical names of the pre-specified persons for the seal of the bank account opened by PuMou Company at Ping An Bank, in order to prove that the three defendants had resold the equity in J* Company.

The court is of the opinion that the registered places of the three defendants in this case are the British Virgin Islands and the United States of America respectively. According to Article 1(1) of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations (I), this case is a foreign-related civil and commercial dispute. Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company is a legal person registered and established in China and applying for bankruptcy in a Chinese court. Zhuhai Mou Company, representing all creditors of the bankrupt enterprise, has filed a subrogation action. Whether it can assert rights through this action shall be governed by the law of the forum, i.e., Chinese law. The parties also unanimously agreed during the trial to apply Chinese law. Therefore, Chinese law shall be applied as the lex causae in this case. According to Article 1(1) of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Temporal Effect of the Application of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China, important facts related to the disputes in this case, such as the transfer of claims, setoff of debts, bankruptcy, and transfer of equity, all occurred after the implementation of the Civil Code. Therefore, the provisions of the Civil Code shall apply to this case.

Based on the opinions of the parties, the issues in dispute in this case are: whether Zhuhai Mou Company has the right to file this action; whether Zhuhai Mou Company can directly assert claims against the three defendants; whether Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company still has any unsatisfied claim against Shanghai Mou Trading Company; and whether Shanghai Mou Trading Company has a claim against the three defendants.

I. Whether Zhuhai Mou Company has the right to file this action

Determining whether Zhuhai Mou Company has the right to file this action requires weighing two factors: whether Zhuhai Mou Company is still a creditor of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company, and whether Zhuhai Mou Company has the right to file this action on behalf of all creditors of Shanghai Mou Entertainment Company.

Whether Zhuhai Company is still a creditor of Shanghai Entertainment Company. According to the facts found, Zhejiang Fiber Company was the guarantor of Zhuhai Company's claim against Shanghai Entertainment Company. In the bankruptcy reorganization case of Zhejiang Fiber Company, the Huzhou Intermediate People's Court ruled to confirm that Zhuhai Company holds an ordinary claim of RMB 80,478,443.86. Pursuant to the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Fiber Company, the ordinary claims of Zhejiang Fiber Company were to be satisfied through a combination of the following: cash consideration paid by the reorganization investor, debt retention, shares used for debt repayment under the equity holder's interest adjustment plan, and trust beneficiary rights. For claims satisfied by capital reserve capitalization to increase shares, the debt-to-share price was RMB 27.8 per share. The satisfaction ratio for ordinary claims of Zhejiang Fiber Company was 100%. Thereafter, Zhuhai Company received RMB 8,047,844.39 in cash and 2,092,440 shares of Zhejiang Fiber Company. According to the stock delivery order dated October 27, 2023, Zhuhai Company acquired the aforesaid shares of Zhejiang Fiber Company at a transaction price of RMB 5.26 per share. Pursuant to Article 92 of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the PRC, which provides: "A reorganization plan approved by a ruling of the people's court is binding on both the debtor and all creditors. A creditor who fails to declare its claim in accordance with the provisions of this Law may not exercise its rights during the implementation period of the reorganization plan; after the implementation of the reorganization plan is completed, it may exercise its rights in accordance with the satisfaction conditions for similar claims as stipulated in the reorganization plan. The rights of a creditor against the debtor's guarantor and other joint and several obligors shall not be affected by the reorganization plan." The reorganization plan binds only the debtor and all creditors. In this case, the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Fiber Company binds only the creditor Zhuhai Company and the debtor Zhejiang Fiber Company. The rights of Zhuhai Company against other joint and several obligors, including Shanghai Entertainment Company, are not affected by the reorganization plan. That is, the pricing of the company's shares in the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Fiber Company and the statement that the satisfaction ratio for ordinary claims of Zhejiang Fiber Company was 100% cannot affect Zhuhai Company's right to seek satisfaction from Shanghai Entertainment Company for the portion not satisfied by Zhejiang Fiber Company. The transaction price of RMB 5.26 per share at which the shares of Zhejiang Fiber Company were transferred to Zhuhai Company is lower than the debt-to-share price of RMB 27.8 per share determined in the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Fiber Company. This debt-to-share price cannot affect Zhuhai Company's claim against Shanghai Entertainment Company. Zhuhai Company's claim has not been fully satisfied, and it has the right to seek satisfaction from Shanghai Entertainment Company for the insufficient portion. Therefore, the claims of the three defendants and Shanghai Entertainment Company that Zhuhai Company's claim against Shanghai Entertainment Company has been fully satisfied in accordance with the Reorganization Plan of Zhejiang Fiber Company are inconsistent with the facts. Zhuhai Company remains a creditor of Shanghai Entertainment Company.

Whether Zhuhai Company has the right to initiate this lawsuit on behalf of all creditors of Shanghai Entertainment Company. Article 23 of Interpretation (II) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the PRC provides: "After a bankruptcy petition is accepted, if a creditor files a lawsuit against the debtor's property as listed in paragraph 1 of Article 21 of this Interpretation with the people's court, the people's court shall not accept it. If a creditor, through the creditors' meeting or the creditors' committee, requests the administrator to recover the debtor's property from the secondary obligor or the debtor's contributors in accordance with the law, and the administrator refuses to do so without justifiable reasons, and the creditors' meeting, in accordance with Article 22 of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law, applies to the people's court to replace the administrator, the people's court shall support such application. If the administrator fails to recover the property, and an individual creditor, on behalf of all creditors, initiates a related lawsuit claiming that the secondary obligor or the debtor's contributors make payment to the debtor or return the debtor's property, or applies for consolidated bankruptcy in accordance with the law, the people's court shall accept the case." According to the above provision, after a bankruptcy petition is accepted, if an individual creditor claims that the debtor of the bankrupt enterprise shall directly pay off its debt to the creditor, the people's court shall not accept the case. However, if the creditor requests the administrator to recover the debtor's property from the secondary obligor or the debtor's contributors in accordance with the law, and the administrator fails to do so, an individual creditor may, on behalf of all creditors, claim that the secondary obligor or the debtor's contributors make payment to the debtor or return the debtor's property. Obtaining the consent or authorization of all creditors through the creditors' meeting or the creditors' committee is not a prerequisite for initiating this lawsuit. Zhuhai Company, being a creditor of Shanghai Entertainment Company, has requested the administrator to recover the debtor's property, and the administrator has expressly declined to do so. Zhuhai Company has also clarified that any property recovered shall be included in the bankruptcy estate of Shanghai Entertainment Company for fair distribution among all creditors in accordance with the law. This complies with the provisions of the aforementioned judicial interpretation. Therefore, Zhuhai Company has the right to initiate this lawsuit on behalf of all creditors.

II. Whether Zhuhai Company can directly assert a claim against the three defendants

This Court holds that, even if Shanghai Entertainment Company holds a claim against Shanghai Trading Company, Zhuhai Company cannot directly assert a claim against the three defendants through a creditor's subrogation action.

First, paragraph 3 of Article 23 of Interpretation (II) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the PRC does not confer on Zhuhai Company the right to directly assert a claim against the secondary obligor of the bankrupt enterprise. According to that provision, an individual creditor may, on behalf of all creditors, initiate a related lawsuit claiming that the secondary obligor or the debtor's contributors make payment to the debtor or return the debtor's property. This provision makes clear that the individual creditor represents all creditors, not the bankrupt enterprise directly. Therefore, it only allows an individual creditor to subrogate, in the name of all creditors, the claim of the bankrupt enterprise against its own debtor. Pursuant to this provision, Zhuhai Company, representing all creditors of Shanghai Entertainment Company, can only assert a claim against the debtor of the bankrupt enterprise Shanghai Entertainment Company, namely, Shanghai Trading Company. Even if Shanghai Trading Company holds a claim against the three defendants, the civil subject entitled to bring a creditor's subrogation action against the three defendants should be the creditor of Shanghai Trading Company, which is Shanghai Entertainment Company, not Zhuhai Company. Therefore, Zhuhai Company's direct assertion of a claim against the three defendants lacks legal basis.

Second, according to the relevant legal provisions on creditor's subrogation, Zhuhai Company cannot claim against the secondary obligor of its own debtor through a two-tier subrogation. Paragraph 1 of Article 535 of the Civil Code of the PRC provides: "Where the debtor neglects to exercise its due claims or the accessory rights related thereto, thereby affecting the realization of the creditor's due claims, the creditor may request the people's court to subrogate, in its own name, the debtor's rights against the counterparty, except for those rights exclusively belonging to the debtor." From a literal interpretation of the provision, the object of a creditor's subrogation right is the debtor's counterparty, which is a civil subject that has a direct legal relationship with the debtor and should be limited to the debtor's own debtor. The provision cannot be interpreted, by going beyond its plain meaning, as including the debtor's secondary obligor or even more remote obligors. Otherwise, an unrestricted expansive interpretation of legal provisions would violate the basic rules of legal interpretation. From the basic principles of contract law, contractual relationships are relative. A contract only creates binding legal effect between the parties to the contract. Civil subjects that have not signed a contract are not bound by it, unless the law provides otherwise. The creditor's subrogation right is a statutory right that appropriately breaks through the principle of privity of contract, and may be exercised by a creditor when the circumstances stipulated in Article 535 of the Civil Code are met. However, such a breakthrough of contractual privity should be strictly limited to situations expressly provided for by law; otherwise, it would impact and disrupt the stability of normal commercial transaction order. Therefore, the creditor's exercise of subrogation rights should not go beyond the circumstances stipulated in Article 535 of the Civil Code. In this case, Zhuhai Company, in the name of all creditors, subrogates the rights of Shanghai Entertainment Company against its counterparty. It may assert property rights against Shanghai Entertainment Company's debtor, Shanghai Trading Company. However, Zhuhai Company did not name Shanghai Trading Company as a defendant; instead, it directly asserted rights against the three defendants, who are the debtors of Shanghai Trading Company. That is, Zhuhai Company seeks to assert a claim against the secondary obligor of Shanghai Entertainment Company through a two-tier subrogation. This claim by Zhuhai Company does not comply with the legal provisions and cannot be sustained.

Since Zhuhai Company has no right to directly assert a claim against the three defendants, this Court will not further examine issues such as the existence of a creditor-debtor relationship between Shanghai Entertainment Company and Shanghai Trading Company, or whether Shanghai Trading Company holds a claim against the three defendants. Similarly, this Court also denies Zhuhai Company's application to request the court to obtain evidence concerning the relevant accounts and retained seal impressions of Pu Company.

Additionally, on October 19, 2022, the Third Intermediate People's Court of Shanghai issued a ruling (2022) Hu 03 Po 420, ruling to accept the application for bankruptcy liquidation of Shanghai Entertainment Company. Pursuant to Article 21 of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the PRC, after a people's court accepts a bankruptcy petition, any civil lawsuit concerning the debtor may only be brought before the people's court that accepted the bankruptcy petition. Zhuhai Company filed this lawsuit on November 28, 2022, which was clearly after the court had accepted the bankruptcy petition. Even if Zhuhai Company was unaware of the bankruptcy liquidation of Shanghai Entertainment Company at the time of filing, on December 16, 2022, the administrator of Shanghai Entertainment Company confirmed Zhuhai Company's claim based on its declaration of creditor's rights, which proves that Zhuhai Company knew before that date that Shanghai Entertainment Company had entered bankruptcy liquidation proceedings. However, Zhuhai Company did not disclose this fact to the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court, which accepted this lawsuit. Furthermore, since Shanghai Entertainment Company is not a party to this case, the Zhuhai Intermediate People's Court could not discover, through service of process, that Shanghai Entertainment Company had entered bankruptcy liquidation proceedings, and thus could not accurately determine whether this case fell under the jurisdiction of the court that accepted the bankruptcy petition. This Court accepted the case for trial due to the typicality and guiding significance of the tort liability action concerning the creditor's claim. However, after the case was filed, it was not until May 28, 2024, when evidence was exchanged between the parties, that this Court, upon presentation of evidence by the three defendants, learned of the bankruptcy liquidation of Shanghai Entertainment Company. After this Court had accepted the case, Zhuhai Company further amended its claims and ultimately determined this case to be a subrogation action on behalf of all creditors of the bankrupt enterprise. This resulted in a case that should have been tried by the court that accepted the bankruptcy petition being escalated for trial by this Court. Such so-called "litigation tactics" by Zhuhai Company are not commendable.

In summary, Zhuhai Company's request to assert claims against the secondary obligor of Shanghai Entertainment Company on behalf of all creditors of Shanghai Entertainment Company lacks factual and legal basis, and this Court denies it. Pursuant to paragraph 1 of Article 1 of the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Code of the PRC with Respect to Temporal Effect, item 1 of Article 1 of the Interpretation (I) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Law of the PRC on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, paragraph 1 of Article 535 of the Civil Code of the PRC, Article 92 of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the PRC, Article 23 of the Provisions (II) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Enterprise Bankruptcy Law of the PRC, and paragraph 1 of Article 15 of the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on the Establishment of International Commercial Courts, the judgment is as follows:

The claims of Zhuhai Company are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 347,935.16 and the preservation fee of RMB 5,000 shall be borne by Zhuhai Company.

This judgment is final.
